newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong's Tung slammed for "red chip" comment.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong's Tung slammed for "red chip" comment.

text.p: Hong Kong's future leader Tung Chee-hwa drew criticism on Thursday after praising a "red chip" company, a firm with China ties that is listed in the territory.
Tung, a Shanghai-born former shipping tycoon, lauded a Hong Kong-listed Shanghai company in a speech to businessmen in the Chinese city on Wednesday.

"We are all familiar with Shanghai Industrial Holdings. Since May 30, 1996, it was listed in Hong Kong. It has been a good performer for H-shares," he said in his speech, which was sent to media organisations by his office.
H-shares are stocks of China-incorporated companies listed in Hong Kong. In fact Shanghai Industrial is not an H-share but a red chip stock.
Tung said the success of Shanghai Industrial Holdings meant that Hong Kong citizens could share the fruits of Shanghai's speedy development and success.

Hong Kong lawmaker Chim Pui-chun, who represents Hong Kong's securities sector, told Reuters Tung was wrong to single out any company as he would be in charge of the territory when the British leave on July 1 and hand it back to China.
"As the Chief Executive, he shouldn't comment on an individual company," Chim said.
Chim advised Tung to be more careful in what he said in future. However he said Hong Kong investors were mature enough not to be blindly led into buying the shares.
Shanghai Industrial Holdings traded 40 cents down at HK$34.20 after Thursday's mid-session. The red chip closed on Wednesday at HK$34.60 (US$4.47).
Hong Kong Democratic Party legislator Huang Chen-ya also said it was inappropriate for government officials to make such remarks.
"No heads of government or officials in the world would say such a thing in praising one company," Huang told Reuters.

Tung, chosen by a China-assembled caucus in December, has already aroused controversy by putting a property tycoon in charge of housing policy when Hong Kong becomes a Special Administrative Region of China in July.
Politicians, both from the pro-democracy camp and the pro-Beijing business lobby, denounced the appointment as posing a potential conflict of interest.
